   181	
   182	# Used to indicate all property classes that are fields defined in ardoq, both buit in and user defined.
   183	aq:FieldType a owl:Class .
   184	
   185	aq:CustomFieldType a owl:Class ;
   186	  rdfs:subClassOf aq:FieldType .
   187	
   188	aq:BuiltInFieldType a owl:Class ;
   189	  rdfs:subClassOf aq:FieldType .
   190	
   191	# The type of all Ardoq fields and hence any RDF reifiers of those statements. The common super class of all ardoq defined Field Types.
   192	aq:Field a owl:Class, owl:DatatypeProperty .
   193	
   194	# A field as it appears in one model: which model it belongs to, and where it sits
   195	# in that model's field list. See the Model Fields section for why this is a
   196	# resource rather than two more predicates on the field type.
   197	aq:ModelField a owl:Class .
   198	```
   199	
   200	## Example
   201	
   202	```text
   203	Verified to be EL/QL/RL/DL valid:
   204	
   205	@prefix rdf:             <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> .
   206	@prefix rdfs:            <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
   207	@prefix owl:             <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
   208	@prefix aq:              <http://data.ardoq.com/meta-model/> .
   209	@prefix aqCommon:        <http://data.ardoq.com/model/common/> .
   210	@prefix aqComponent:     <http://data.ardoq.com/instances/components/> .
   211	@prefix aqReference:     <http://data.ardoq.com/instances/references/> .
   212	@prefix aqComponentType: <http://data.ardoq.com/model/component-types/> .
   213	@prefix aqReferenceType: <http://data.ardoq.com/model/reference-types/> .
   214	
   215	### Meta Model
   216	aq:ComponentType a owl:Class .
   217	aq:ReferenceType a owl:Class .
   218	aq:Component a owl:Class .
   219	aq:Reference a owl:Class, owl:ObjectProperty .
   220	aq:FieldType a owl:Class .
   221	aq:CustomFieldType a owl:Class ;
   222	  rdfs:subClassOf aq:FieldType .
   223	aq:BuiltInFieldType a owl:Class ;
   224	  rdfs:subClassOf aq:FieldType .
   225	aq:Field a owl:Class, owl:DatatypeProperty .
   226	aq:ModelField a owl:Class .
   227	
   228	### Built In Model Constructs
   229	
   230	aqCommon:id a aq:BuiltInFieldType, owl:Class, owl:DatatypeProperty ;
   231	  rdfs:subClassOf aq:Field ;
   232	  rdfs:subPropertyOf aq:Field .
   233	
   234	# aqCommon:name, created, description, createdBy, all follow the same pattern.
   235	# These are all pulled from the component and reference table in Ardoq
   236	
   237	### Examples
   238	
   239	# This is an example of a Ardoq defined component type.
   240	# For _reasons_ it's split across a global and a workspace local type.
   241	# It is itself a component type of course, but it's also a subclass of
   242	# aq:Component, such that all instances of this type are also instances of aq:Component.
   243	aqComponentType:global001 a aq:ComponentType, owl:Class ;
   244	  rdfs:subClassOf aq:Component .
   245	
   246	# The local type is a subclass of the global type, so that any instance
   247	# are also instances of the global type.
   248	aqComponentType:local001 a aq:ComponentType, owl:Class ;
   249	  rdfs:subClassOf aqComponentType:global001 .
   250	
   251	# Example of a user-defined component.
   252	aqComponent:001 a aqComponentType:local001 ;
   253	  aqCommon:id "001" .
   254	
   255	## References
   256	
   257	# Example of a user-defined reference type. Same as for component types, it's
   258	# split into local and global. It's both a class and a property, because it
   259	# will be used as predicate for the reified triple, and type for the reifier.
   260	# It's also both a subclass and subproperty of aq:Reference, so that
   261	# instances and triples get the relevant supertype and superproperty inferred.
   262	aqReferenceType:global001 a aq:ReferenceType, owl:ObjectProperty, owl:Class ;
   263	  rdfs:subClassOf aq:Reference ;
   264	  rdfs:subPropertyOf aq:Reference .
   265	
   266	aqReferenceType:local001 a aq:ReferenceType, owl:ObjectProperty, owl:Class ;
   267	  rdfs:subClassOf aqReferenceType:global001 ;
   268	  rdfs:subPropertyOf aqReferenceType:global001 .
   269	
   270	# Here's an example of a reference. The reference entity is the reifier, but
   271	# the triple it reifies is necessary to be able to traverse the graph.
   272	aqComponent:001 aqReferenceType:local001 aqComponent:001 ~ aqReference:001 {|
   273	  a aqReferenceType:local001 ;
   274	  aqCommon:id "001"
   275	|} .
   276	
   277	# With this, we should have inferred triples like:
   278	#   aqComponent:001 aq:Reference aqComponent:001
   279	#   aqReference:001 a aq:Reference
   280	#   aqComponent:001 a aq:Component
   281	# These can all be inferred by RDFS reasoning, but we have taken care to ensure
   282	# the model is also OWL 2 EL/QL/RL/DL compliant, so more advanced reasoning can
   283	# be applied if needed
   284	```
   285	
   286	## Users
   287	
   288	A user is the author of a row: `common/createdBy` and `common/lastModifiedBy` are
   289	`owl:ObjectProperty` edges to a `common/User`, not string literals.
   290	
   291	The edit pair is named asymmetrically: the time is `common/lastUpdated` and the
   292	user is `common/lastModifiedBy`, which is how the rest of the platform names
   293	them and what the source columns are called. Advanced search filters the user
   294	under "last modified by", so a predicate named after the timestamp would match
   295	nothing and the endpoint would answer zero rows with an HTTP 200.
   296	
   297	```text
   298	
   299	# User class:
   300	  http://data.ardoq.com/model/common/User
   301	
   302	# User instance:
   303	  http://data.ardoq.com/instances/users/<user_account._id>
   304	
   305	# Properties:
   306	  http://data.ardoq.com/model/common/id      user_account._id
   307	  http://data.ardoq.com/model/common/name    user_account.name
   308	
   309	# Edges to it, from a component, a reference reifier or a workspace:
   310	  http://data.ardoq.com/model/common/createdBy
   311	  http://data.ardoq.com/model/common/lastModifiedBy
   312	
   313	```
   314	
   315	**The users come from `public.user_account` in the Ardoq settings database**, the
   316	one `GL_SYNC_ARDOQ_DB_URI` points at. An Ardoq org schema has no `user` table: its
   317	audit columns carry a bare `user_account._id` and nothing else, so the display name
   318	a person searches by is reachable only from there. The name is the reason to write
   319	the resource at all — a User carrying only its id told a query nothing the
   320	`createdBy` edge had not already said.
   321	
   322	Which rows of that table is the whole of the design, because the settings database
   323	is shared by every organisation on an installation. Two things scope it, and both
   324	are needed:
   325	
   326	- **The organisation's people** — `organization.members` and
   327	  `organization.contributors`, jsonb objects keyed by `user_account._id`. This is
   328	  what puts a person in the graph before they have touched anything.
   329	- **The organisation's authors** — every id in an audit column of its schema,
   330	  member or not. Without this an author who has left would resolve to nothing and
   331	  their `createdBy` edges would point at an IRI carrying no triples, which the SHACL
   332	  shape declaring `createdBy`'s range to be `User` makes a violation rather than
   333	  merely a gap. Advanced search resolves an author the same way: a join to the users
   334	  table with no membership filter.
   335	
   336	Neither half reaches outside the organisation: one is its own row, the other its own
   337	data.
   338	
   339	**An author id with no row still gets its resource**, carrying the id and no name.
   340	Only a hard-deleted account gets there — `user_account` has a delete trigger, and
   341	deleting the row does not clear the id out of the audit columns of everything that
   342	person touched, so those ids outlive the row for ever. The resource is written
   343	anyway because the `createdBy` edge pointing at it already exists, and the SHACL
   344	shape for `createdBy` declares its range to be `User`: an edge into an IRI carrying
   345	no triples is a violation on every row that person authored, which is strictly worse
   346	than a resource with no name. The last known name is still in
   347	`user_account__history`, but the syncer's Postgres role has no grant on that
   348	table.
   349	
   350	One consequence worth knowing: a deleted account and a live user whose `name` is
   351	null produce exactly the same two triples, so the graph cannot tell them apart.
   352	
   353	`user_account.name` is nullable, so a user without one gets no `common/name` triple
   354	rather than an empty literal. Nothing else on the row is read — it also holds an
   355	email address, a password hash and SAML/SCIM identifiers, none of which belong in a
   356	graph store.
   357	
   358	A user is written once per target rather than once per row, for the same reason the
   359	model-level triples are: both bulk paths send `X-GraphLake-Skip-Duplicate-Check`, so
   360	a resource re-asserted per component would be *stored* per component. There is no
   361	update or delete mapping for one — a full sync rewrites the directory, and the
   362	streaming path re-asserts an author when it sees one of their rows.
   363	
   364	The id is percent-escaped when minting the IRI. Unlike a component or reference id
   365	it is minted from an audit column as often as from the user row, and nothing
   366	validates an audit column, so one stray space would otherwise produce a malformed
   367	IRI and fail the whole update.
   368	
   369	Example source rows:
   370	
   371	```text
   372	user_account._id          u-ada
   373	user_account.name         Ada Lovelace
   374	
   375	component._id             app-001
   376	component.createdBy       u-ada
   377	component.lastModifiedBy  u-grace
   378	```
   379	
   380	Example triples:
   381	
   382	```turtle
   383	aqUser:u-ada a aqCommon:User ;
   384	  aqCommon:id   "u-ada" ;
   385	  aqCommon:name "Ada Lovelace" .
   386	
   387	aqComponent:app-001
   388	  aqCommon:createdBy      aqUser:u-ada ;
   389	  aqCommon:lastModifiedBy aqUser:u-grace .
   390	```
   391	
   392	Both edges are cleared by `del_component_metadata` and `del_reference_metadata`,
   393	alongside `rdf:type`, `common/parent` and `common/workspace`, because
   394	`del_all_about` removes only literal-object triples: a row that changed hands would
   395	otherwise name both authors.
   396	
   397	Being object-valued has one model-level consequence. `common/createdBy` and
   398	`common/lastModifiedBy` are no longer `aq:BuiltInFieldType` and no longer sit under
   399	`aq:Field`. `aq:Field` is an `owl:DatatypeProperty`, and OWL 2 DL requires object
   400	and data properties to be disjoint, so an object-valued built-in cannot be a
   401	sub-property of it — the same reason `common/parent` and `common/workspace` are not.
   402	Their SHACL shapes are `sh:class common/User` rather than `sh:datatype xsd:string`.
   403	
   404	`global_field.type = 'User'` values are still `xsd:string`. They are user ids too
   405	and should become edges to these same resources; that is not mapped yet.
   406	
   407	### Emitting a user exactly once
   408	
   409	The resources are emitted **once per target**, never per row. Both bulk paths send
   410	`X-GraphLake-Skip-Duplicate-Check`, which turns off GraphLake's duplicate check, so
   411	a type triple asserted once per component would be *stored* once per component: on
   412	this repo's dev org that is 33,716 copies of one triple for a single user. Each
   413	path uses its own mechanism:
   414	
   415	```text
   416	full sync         one directory read, before components, per target (main and each
   417	                  branch, since each commits by MOVEing its own graph over the
   418	                  target's live graph). The author half of its scope is a `select
   419	                  distinct` over the audit columns of the live tables
   420	history backfill  the same, with the author pass reading the history mirrors as
   421	                  well. Recorded once before the first month as one `user:<id>`
   422	                  entity in the carried state, and written nowhere else: a month's
   423	                  snapshot is materialised from that state, and the backfill does
   424	                  not touch the head
   425	CDC streaming     per row, resolving each author against the settings database
   426	                  through a cache that holds misses as well as hits. This is the
   427	                  only path that can add a user between full syncs: the CDC stream
   428	                  carries the org schema, and the directory is elsewhere. It does
   429	                  not skip the duplicate check, so the store collapses the repeats
   430	```
   431	
   432	The two author passes differ deliberately. A full sync writes live state, so a
   433	live-only pass is right. Replay materialises entities that have since been deleted —
   434	a component removed last year is written into every month before its deletion — and
   435	its author may appear in no live row, so a live-only pass there would leave that
   436	component's `createdBy` edge pointing at an untyped IRI.
   437

    24	// The three levels of the vocabulary. See the "RDF namespaces" section of the
    25	// README for what belongs in each.

    28		// classes saying what kind of thing it is, and the two predicates carrying its
    29		// machine-readable identity. No SHACL shape targets them.
    30		MetaModelNamespace = "http://data.ardoq.com/meta-model/"
    31	
    32		// ModelNamespace holds the model itself: the types, field types, shared
    33		// predicates and the shapes that constrain them.
    34		ModelNamespace = "http://data.ardoq.com/model/"
    35	
    36		// InstancesNamespace holds the individuals a customer created.
    37		InstancesNamespace = "http://data.ardoq.com/instances/"
    38	)
    39

    42		ComponentTypeNamespace = ModelNamespace + "component-types/"
    43		ReferenceTypeNamespace = ModelNamespace + "reference-types/"

    45		CommonNamespace        = ModelNamespace + "common/"

    49		// field_id_by_model._id. See ModelFieldClassIRI for why that is a resource of
    50		// its own rather than more predicates on the field type.
    51		ModelFieldNamespace = ModelNamespace + "model-fields/"
    52	
    53		ComponentNamespace = InstancesNamespace + "components/"
    54		ReferenceNamespace = InstancesNamespace + "references/"
    55		TagNamespace       = InstancesNamespace + "tags/"
    56		WorkspaceNamespace = InstancesNamespace + "workspaces/"
    57		UserNamespace      = InstancesNamespace + "users/"

    68		ReferenceTypeClassIRI = MetaModelNamespace + "ReferenceType"

    74		// row mints it and no shape targets it.

    78		// class. CustomFieldType and BuiltInFieldType split those into the ones
    79		// defined in global_field and the ones in Ardoq's own vocabulary. Field is the
    80		// super-property every field property sits under, so "every field of this
    81		// thing" is one traversal.
    82		FieldTypeClassIRI        = MetaModelNamespace + "FieldType"
    83		CustomFieldTypeClassIRI  = MetaModelNamespace + "CustomFieldType"
    84		BuiltInFieldTypeClassIRI = MetaModelNamespace + "BuiltInFieldType"

    88		// field_id_by_model row joining a global_field to a model, and the thing
    89		// Ardoq's own API calls a field.

    92		// facts it carries are per model, not per field. A global_field is org-wide and
    93		// its property IRI is minted from global_field._id, but its position in the
    94		// field list is not: `review_date` sits in twenty-five models with orders 0

    96		// multi-valued with nothing to say which model each value belongs to, which is

content.content:
## Sync Behavior

### RDF namespaces

`model-mapping.md` is the specification for how Ardoq rows become RDF.
`pkg/syncer/testdata/model_mapping_report.ttl` is the same mapping rendered for a
small dataset, annotated with the table and column each triple comes from; run
`make mapping-report` to print it.

Three levels are kept apart:

| Namespace | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `http://data.ardoq.com/meta-model/` | The meta level: `Component`, `Reference`, `ComponentType`, `ReferenceType`, `Tag`, `Workspace`, `FieldType`, `CustomFieldType`, `BuiltInFieldType`, `Field`. These say what kind of thing a model construct is. It also holds the predicates a model construct is identified by: `id` and `name`, plus `modelId`, `componentTypeId` and `referenceTypeId` — the legacy pair a concrete type publishes for Ardoq's pre-GraphLake code. No SHACL shape targets any of them. It also holds `ModelField`, the class of a field's placement in one model, and the four predicates saying what a field is beyond its identity: `fieldType` and `numberFormatOptions` on the shared definition, `order` and `field` on the placement. And it holds `color`, `icon`, `image` and `shape`: how a component type is drawn, which every component of it inherits. The per-component override is under `model/common/`, because its subject is an individual rather than a class. |
| `http://data.ardoq.com/model/` | The model itself: `component-types/`, `reference-types/`, `field-types/`, `model-fields/`, `common/`, and the `shapes/` that constrain it. `common/User` is the one class here, because a user classifies no model construct. |
| `http://data.ardoq.com/instances/` | The individuals a customer created: `components/`, `references/`, `tags/`, `workspaces/`, `users/`. |

**Breaking.** Every IRI a store already holds is affected:

- the meta-level classes moved from `model/` to `meta-model/`, so
  `rdfs:subClassOf` chains in an older store point at classes nothing asserts
- components, references and tags moved from `model/components/`,
  `model/reference-statements/` and `model/tags/` to `instances/components/`,
  `instances/references/` and `instances/tags/`
- the `common/parent` object-property shape IRI changed, because it is minted by
  hashing the class it constrains
- a model construct's identity moved from `common/id` and `common/name` to
  `meta-model/id` and `meta-model/name`. Those two `common/` predicates are
  themselves built-in field types, so a field type described with them was described
  using itself, and `?s common/id ?id` returned classes and individuals jumbled
  together. Component types, reference types and field types now answer on the
  meta-level pair; components, reference reifiers, workspaces, tags and users keep
  the `common/` one, where the id really is a field value

Every target store must be re-bootstrapped. There is no migration.

### Full sync

For each schema in `GL_SYNC_SCHEMAS`, the current-state load:

## Sync Behavior

### RDF namespaces

`model-mapping.md` is the specification for how Ardoq rows become RDF.
`pkg/syncer/testdata/model_mapping_report.ttl` is the same mapping rendered for a
small dataset, annotated with the table and column each triple comes from; run
`make mapping-report` to print it.

Three levels are kept apart:

| Namespace | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `http://data.ardoq.com/meta-model/` | The meta level: `Component`, `Reference`, `ComponentType`, `ReferenceType`, `Tag`, `Workspace`, `FieldType`, `CustomFieldType`, `BuiltInFieldType`, `Field`. These say what kind of thing a model construct is. It also holds the predicates a model construct is identified by: `id` and `name`, plus `modelId`, `componentTypeId` and `referenceTypeId` — the legacy pair a concrete type publishes for Ardoq's pre-GraphLake code. No SHACL shape targets any of them. It also holds `ModelField`, the class of a field's placement in one model, and the four predicates saying what a field is beyond its identity: `fieldType` and `numberFormatOptions` on the shared definition, `order` and `field` on the placement. And it holds `color`, `icon`, `image` and `shape`: how a component type is drawn, which every component of it inherits. The per-component override is under `model/common/`, because its subject is an individual rather than a class. |
| `http://data.ardoq.com/model/` | The model itself: `component-types/`, `reference-types/`, `field-types/`, `model-fields/`, `common/`, and the `shapes/` that constrain it. `common/User` is the one class here, because a user classifies no model construct. |
| `http://data.ardoq.com/instances/` | The individuals a customer created: `components/`, `references/`, `tags/`, `workspaces/`, `users/`. |

**Breaking.** Every IRI a store already holds is affected:

- the meta-level classes moved from `model/` to `meta-model/`, so
  `rdfs:subClassOf` chains in an older store point at classes nothing asserts
- components, references and tags moved from `model/components/`,
  `model/reference-statements/` and `model/tags/` to `instances/components/`,
  `instances/references/` and `instances/tags/`
- the `common/parent` object-property shape IRI changed, because it is minted by
  hashing the class it constrains
- a model construct's identity moved from `common/id` and `common/name` to
  `meta-model/id` and `meta-model/name`. Those two `common/` predicates are
  themselves built-in field types, so a field type described with them was described
  using itself, and `?s common/id ?id` returned classes and individuals jumbled
  together. Component types, reference types and field types now answer on the
  meta-level pair; components, reference reifiers, workspaces, tags and users keep
  the `common/` one, where the id really is a field value

Every target store must be re-bootstrapped. There is no migration.

content.content:
## Workspaces

Workspaces are modelled explicitly and also as a string property on components and references. This is to facilitate explicit use of workspace ids and be backwards compatible with gremlin graph queries which treat workspace as a string property on nodes.

```text

# Workspace class:
  http://data.ardoq.com/meta-model/Workspace

# Workspace instance:
  http://data.ardoq.com/instances/workspaces/<workspace._id>

# Edge to the workspace, from a component or a reference reifier:
  http://data.ardoq.com/model/common/workspace

# The same value as a literal, for gremlin parity:
  http://data.ardoq.com/model/common/rootWorkspace

```

`Workspace` sits at the meta level next to `Tag`, for the same reason: its members
are individuals a customer created, not model constructs. No concrete type row
mints it and no shape targets it.

The literal and the edge are two IRIs, not one. OWL 2 DL keeps object and data
properties disjoint — "no IRI is declared to be both object and data property" —
so `common/rootWorkspace` stays the `owl:DatatypeProperty` gremlin queries read,
and `common/workspace` is the `owl:ObjectProperty` that points at the resource.
Both are built from the one `rootWorkspace` column, so they cannot name different
workspaces.

A workspace individual carries the same built-ins a component does, rather than a
second spelling of name and description:

```text
workspace._id            aqCommon:id
workspace.name           aqCommon:name
workspace.description    aqCommon:description
workspace.created        aqCommon:created,       xsd:dateTime
workspace.createdBy      aqCommon:createdBy
workspace.lastUpdated    aqCommon:lastUpdated,   xsd:dateTime
workspace.lastModifiedBy aqCommon:lastModifiedBy
```

Example source rows:

```text
workspace._id            ws-apps
workspace.name           Applications
workspace.description    Business application landscape

component._id            app-001
component.rootWorkspace  ws-apps

reference._id            ref-deploy-001
reference.rootWorkspace  ws-apps
```

Example triples:

```turtle
aqWorkspace:ws-apps a aqModel:Workspace ;
  aqCommon:id "ws-apps" ;
  aqCommon:name "Applications" ;
  aqCommon:description "Business application landscape" .

aqComponent:app-001
  aqCommon:rootWorkspace "ws-apps" ;
  aqCommon:workspace aqWorkspace:ws-apps .

aqRefStatement:SHA1
  aqCommon:rootWorkspace "ws-apps" ;
  aqCommon:workspace aqWorkspace:ws-apps .
```

A reference's workspace is its own `reference.rootWorkspace` column, not its
source component's, and it lands on the reifier — the node that also carries the
edge's id and properties. `reference.targetWorkspace` also exists in the source
and is not mapped: a cross-workspace reference is currently found through its
target component's workspace.

Like `hasTag`, `common/workspace` carries no `rdfs:domain`, because its subject may
be a component or a reference reifier. Its range is stated in SHACL, through the
built-in property shape linked onto each concrete component type and each concrete
reference type node shape.

The inbound edges are not built from the workspace row. Membership lives on the
component and reference rows, so each entity asserts its own edge — the mirror
image of tags, where membership is on the tag row. A workspace delete therefore
retracts only the workspace's own triples; the edges pointing at it are cleared
when their entities are updated or deleted, by `del_component_metadata` and
`del_reference_metadata`. Those two clear `common/workspace` by pattern for the
same reason they clear `common/parent`: `del_all_about` removes only
literal-object triples, so a component that moved workspace would otherwise
assert both the old and the new one.

There is no `branched_workspace` table in Ardoq — workspaces are not branched.
It does not come up: Ardoq branches are not synced at all, so the `workspace`
rows are asserted into `main` and nowhere else.

## Built In Data Properties

Built-in literal component fields are `owl:DatatypeProperty` values with domain `Component`, range constraints, and SHACL data-property shapes:

```text
common/id            label "Ardoq OID",    range xsd:string
common/componentKey  label "Ardoq ID",     range xsd:string
common/name          label "Name",         range xsd:string
common/description   label "Description",  range xsd:string
common/created       label "Created",      range xsd:dateTime
common/lastUpdated   label "Last updated", range xsd:dateTime
common/rootWorkspace label "Workspace",    range xsd:string
common/color         label "Color",        range xsd:string
common/icon          label "Icon",         range xsd:string
common/image         label "Image",        range xsd:string
common/shape         label "Shape",        range xsd:string
common/order         label "Order",        range xsd:decimal
```

And the object-valued built-ins, whose labels come from the same table:

```text
common/createdBy      label "Created by",  range common/User
common/lastModifiedBy label "Updated by",  range common/User
common/workspace      label "Workspace",   range Workspace
common/parent         label "ardoq_parent", range Component   (see below)
common/hasTag         label "Tags",        range Tag
```

### The four predicates every field type carries

A field type carries the same four things: two for a machine to match on, two for a
person to read.

```turtle
aqFieldType:gf-cost
  aqModel:id   "gf-cost" ;              # machine-readable id
  aqModel:name "cost" ;                 # machine-readable name
  rdfs:label   "Cost" ;                 # human-readable label
  rdfs:comment "Annual licence cost" .  # human-readable description
```

These four are the identity, and every field type has them. A *custom* field type
also carries what its `global_field` row says the field is — `aqModel:fieldType` and
`aqModel:numberFormatOptions`, described under Global Fields — and a built-in
carries neither, having no row to read them from. Where the field sits in a model's
field list is on a separate resource again; see Model Fields.

Built-ins take the same shape:

```turtle
aqCommon:name a aqModel:BuiltInFieldType, owl:Class, owl:DatatypeProperty ;
  aqModel:id   "name" ;
  aqModel:name "name" ;
  rdfs:label   "Name" .

aqCommon:id a aqModel:BuiltInFieldType, owl:Class, owl:DatatypeProperty ;
  aqModel:id   "id" ;
  aqModel:name "id" ;
  rdfs:label   "Ardoq OID" .
```

One query then answers "what is this field called" without knowing which kind it is.

**The identity is at the meta level, not under `common/`.** `common/id` and
`common/name` are themselves built-in field types, so describing a field type with
them described it using itself: the graph held `common/name common/name "name"`.
`meta-model/id` and `meta-model/name` are the syncer's own vocabulary for describing
a model construct, declared as `owl:AnnotationProperty` — the bucket `rdfs:label` is
in — because their subjects are classes and properties rather than individuals.

content.content:
`row_to_json` payload, where a number arrives as a `float64` and Go's default
rendering switches to exponent form once the exponent reaches the digit count
(`1234567` renders `1.234567e+06`). Two spellings of one order are two triples for
one fact: the diff that moves a component would churn a delete and an insert on an
order nobody changed, and a consumer matching the literal would miss whichever
spelling it was not holding. One renderer serves all three paths, exactly as
`idValueAsString` does for the numeric id columns.

**A value that is not a number writes no triple.** This is where order parts company
with the audit timestamps, which fall back to a plain string: a `lastUpdated` Ardoq
never validated really can hold unparseable text, whereas both order columns are
numeric and NOT NULL in every org schema. A string under a predicate whose shape says
`xsd:decimal` would be reported by SHACL as if the value were the problem, so the
value is dropped and logged instead.

**`common/order` is not `meta-model/order`.** They are different facts about
different subjects: this one is where a component or a reference sits among its
siblings, and `meta-model/order` is where a field sits in one model's field list,
whose subject is a `ModelField` (see Model Fields). Only the field-level one is
read from `field_id_by_model._order` — a third `_order` column, and a third type
again, which is why the schema declaration names it per table.

**Filter on it by value, not by term.** A bound literal in a triple pattern matches
by term, so `1` — which is `"1"^^xsd:integer` — does not match an order:

```sparql
# matches nothing: "1"^^xsd:integer is not "1"^^xsd:decimal
ASK { ?ref aqCommon:order 1 }

# matches: = is defined over numeric values, across datatypes
ASK { ?ref aqCommon:order ?order . FILTER(?order = 1) }
```

This is not specific to order — every `Number` custom field carries `xsd:decimal`
and behaves the same way — but it is what a consumer filtering on order has to do.
Both directions are asserted in the container rig, so a consumer reading this can
rely on them.

Example for `common/name`:

```turtle
aqCommon:name a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
  a aq:BuiltInFieldType
  rdfs:domain aqModel:Component ;
  rdfs:range xsd:string .

aqShape:54dcd78d-dcaf-579b-ae22-1dc9441dc833 a sh:NodeShape ;
  sh:targetClass aqModel:Component ;
  sh:property aqShape:4ee11288-8350-5275-ad74-f52c5af3628c .

aqShape:4ee11288-8350-5275-ad74-f52c5af3628c a sh:PropertyShape ;
  sh:path aqCommon:name ;
  sh:datatype xsd:string .
```

`common/parent` is an `owl:ObjectProperty`, because component parent triples point to another component resource. Its `rdfs:label` is `ardoq_parent`, not `parent` — the one built-in whose label is not Ardoq's display wording. Its `common/name` is still `parent`, so a query for the field by name is unaffected:

```turtle
aqCommon:parent a owl:ObjectProperty ;
  rdfs:label "ardoq_parent" ;
  rdfs:domain aqModel:Component ;
  rdfs:range aqModel:Component .

aqShape:54dcd78d-dcaf-579b-ae22-1dc9441dc833
  sh:property aqShape:edd0a4c4-2c8d-5bb0-bb64-c4894c3aef3b .

aqShape:edd0a4c4-2c8d-5bb0-bb64-c4894c3aef3b a sh:PropertyShape ;
  sh:path aqCommon:parent ;
  sh:class aqModel:Component .
```

## Component Types

Each `component_type` row creates two class levels:

```text
Component
  -> common component name class, minted from component_type.name
    -> concrete component type class, identified by component_type._id
```

Example source row:

```text
component_type._id         ct-7f3a9d2c
component_type.name        Application
component_type.description Business application final schema
component_type.color       #af73ff
component_type.icon        svg_sprite_application
component_type.shape       item
component_type.image       (null)
```

Example triples:

```turtle
aqCompType:a0a27382-298e-574f-a571-dea6ea4cd2ca a rdfs:Class, owl:Class ;

toolUseResult.stdout:
`row_to_json` payload, where a number arrives as a `float64` and Go's default
rendering switches to exponent form once the exponent reaches the digit count
(`1234567` renders `1.234567e+06`). Two spellings of one order are two triples for

order nobody changed, and a consumer matching the literal would miss whichever
spelling it was not holding. One renderer serves all three paths, exactly as

**A value that is not a number writes no triple.** This is where order parts company
with the audit timestamps, which fall back to a plain string: a `lastUpdated` Ardoq
never validated really can hold unparseable text, whereas both order columns are
numeric and NOT NULL in every org schema. A string under a predicate whose shape says

value is dropped and logged instead.

**`common/order` is not `meta-model/order`.** They are different facts about
different subjects: this one is where a component or a reference sits among its
siblings, and `meta-model/order` is where a field sits in one model's field list,
whose subject is a `ModelField` (see Model Fields). Only the field-level one is

again, which is why the schema declaration names it per table.

by term, so `1` — which is `"1"^^xsd:integer` — does not match an order:

```sparql

# matches: = is defined over numeric values, across datatypes

and behaves the same way — but it is what a consumer filtering on order has to do.
Both directions are asserted in the container rig, so a consumer reading this can
rely on them.

### Date Ranges

Ardoq has no range field. A "Date Range" or "Date Time Range" in the UI is **two
`global_field` rows**, distinguished by a suffix on both the machine name and the
display label:

content.content:
```text
global_field  gf-live-start  name=live_start_date  label=Live.StartDate  type=Date
              gf-live-end    name=live_end_date    label=Live.EndDate    type=Date
```

Ardoq's frontend collapses the pair into one field of type `DateOnlyRange` or
`DateTimeRange`, and the syncer does the same, so the graph shows the one field a
person sees rather than the two rows the database holds.

**The start row publishes the whole range, under its own IRI.** That identity is
Ardoq's choice, not this repo's: `collapse-date-range-field` gives the collapsed
field the start field's `_id` and `field_view` reports it, so a consumer holding a
range field's id from Ardoq's API matches the IRI here. It also means the field's
model-field links and type constraints need no rewriting.

**The end row publishes nothing at all** — no property, no shape, no model field,
no type constraint. Its dates are inside the start field's interval literal, so a
property of its own would be the same fact under a second predicate.

```turtle
aqFieldType:gf-live-start a aqModel:CustomFieldType, owl:Class, owl:DatatypeProperty ;
  aqModel:id        "gf-live-start" ;   # still the start row's _id
  aqModel:name      "live" ;            # the suffix removed
  aqModel:fieldType "DateOnlyRange" ;   # Ardoq's word for the collapsed field
  rdfs:label        "Live" .

aqShape:ef16e9dc-b8a6-55e7-b25a-8104184f799b a sh:PropertyShape ;
  sh:path aqFieldType:gf-live-start ;
  sh:datatype <http://graphlake.net/types/iso8601-date-interval> .
```

A value is one ISO 8601 interval: two endpoints separated by a slash, both dates
or both dateTimes. **Either side may be empty**, because a range with only a start
is ordinary data — a subscription nobody has cancelled — rather than an incomplete
row:

```turtle
aqComponent:app-001
  aqFieldType:gf-live-start "2024-01-01/2024-12-31"^^glType:iso8601-date-interval .

# 2024-01-01/    still running, no end date
# /2024-12-31    ended, no recorded start
```

Neither half set writes no triple. `"/"` carries no information and GraphLake
rejects it outright, which would fail the whole update it arrived in.

The two endpoints are rendered for the field's own collapsed type rather than for
whatever each value looks like, because GraphLake rejects an interval whose sides
are different kinds. A `DateOnlyRange` holding a value with a time in it therefore
writes two dates, the same truncation an ordinary `Date` field makes.

`gl:intervalStart` and `gl:intervalEnd` read the endpoints back as typed
`xsd:date` / `xsd:dateTime` literals, and an open end comes back unbound:

```sparql
PREFIX gl: <http://graphlake.net/functions/>
SELECT ?c WHERE {
  ?c aqFieldType:gf-live-start ?live .
  FILTER(gl:intervalStart(?live) <= "2024-06-01"^^xsd:date)
  FILTER(!BOUND(gl:intervalEnd(?live)) || gl:intervalEnd(?live) >= "2024-06-01"^^xsd:date)
}
```

**Which rows are endpoints is decided from the one row**, by the type, the name
suffix and the label suffix together — Ardoq's own test
(`date-range-start-field?`). The label matters as much as the name: a customer may
legitimately call a plain `Date` field `contract_end_date`, and only the
`.EndDate` label says the frontend created it as half of a range.

Deciding per row rather than by pairing the two is deliberate. Pairing would mean
holding the sibling's state on all three ingest paths, and on the streaming path
the events arrive one at a time, so a start field seen before its end existed
would publish the uncollapsed form and need retracting later. Two things follow
from the choice:

- An **orphaned end row** — one whose start row is missing, which Ardoq's own
  metamodel refactoring can leave behind — publishes nothing, rather than
  reverting to a plain `Date` field. Its values go with it.
- An **orphaned start row** publishes a range whose values are always open at the
  end.

One narrow gap is left on the streaming path. Renaming an ordinary `Date` field
*into* an endpoint retracts its property, but a model field or type constraint
already pointing at it is only corrected by the next full sync: nothing emits an
event for those rows when the field they name is renamed.

### `aqModel:fieldType` Is Ardoq's Word, Not The XSD One

The datatype table above is lossy in one direction. Seven Ardoq types — `Text`,
`TextArea`, `List`, `SelectMultipleList`, `Email`, `User` and `File` — all become
`xsd:string`, so a consumer reading only `sh:datatype` cannot tell a free-text field
from a single-select list from an email address. Advanced search needs that
distinction to choose an editor and a filter for the field.

So `global_field.type` is published verbatim as well as derived:

```turtle
aqFieldType:lifecycle
  aqModel:fieldType "List" .           # global_field.type, unaltered
```

Both, not one: `sh:datatype` is what a value must validate against, `aqModel:fieldType`
is what Ardoq calls the field. A field with no type writes no triple.

### `aqModel:numberFormatOptions`

`global_field.numberFormatOptions` is a jsonb column carried as one string literal.
It holds a format name on most fields and an option object on some, so both shapes
reach the graph:

```turtle
aqFieldType:revenue
  aqModel:fieldType           "Number" ;
  aqModel:numberFormatOptions "currencyUSD" .   # jsonb string "currencyUSD"

aqFieldType:cost
  aqModel:fieldType           "Number" ;
  aqModel:numberFormatOptions "{\"decimals\":2,\"suffix\":\" USD\"}" .
```

One literal rather than a predicate per option. The option set is Ardoq's and this
repo does not own it, so decomposing it would invent vocabulary here and silently
drop whatever Ardoq adds to it next.

**The literal is the column's value, not its JSON serialisation.** A jsonb string is
serialised with its quoting — `"currencyUSD"` — and that quoting is Postgres's
spelling rather than part of the value, so it is not published. Ardoq's own code
writes and reads a format name as a plain string, and a consumer given
`"currencyUSD"` would not recognise it.

**The lexical form is canonicalised, and has to be.** The column reaches the mapper
in two shapes: as text on the snapshot path, which is how pgx renders jsonb, and
decoded on the CDC and history paths. Neither an object nor a scalar agrees across
the two on its own.

- Postgres orders jsonb keys by length then bytes and Go's encoder orders them
  lexicographically, so `{"suffix":…,"decimals":…}` read by a full sync and the same
  object read from a CDC event would be two different literals.
- A string carries its quoting in the serialised text and none once decoded, so one
  format would reach the graph as `"currencyUSD"` through a full resync and
  `currencyUSD` through a streamed update, and both forms can be live in one
  organisation at once because it depends on which route last wrote each field.
  Nothing in the graph tells the two apart, since both are plain string literals.

Both shapes are therefore decoded and rendered the one way. The decode is
deliberately the lossy one — plain `json.Unmarshal`, numbers through float64 —
because the decoded path has already been through it and the text path has to agree
with the less precise of the two. Since a field-type update is a byte-for-byte diff
of the before and after triples, two spellings would also churn a delete and an
insert the first time any unrelated column changed.

An absent, null or empty value writes no triple, so a query cannot match a field
with no formatting against one whose formatting is `{}`. Text that is not JSON at
all is kept as it stands rather than dropped: it is what a decoded string scalar
looks like arriving, the column is unconstrained, and losing a value silently is
worse than carrying an odd one.

### Field Values On Instances

A field's values, on components and on reference reifiers, are written as literals
typed with the datatype from the table above. `xsd:string` is left implicit: a
plain literal already has that datatype in RDF, so it is not spelled out.

```turtle
aqComponent:app-001
  aqFieldType:gf-annual-cost "73218541"^^xsd:decimal ;   # Number
  aqFieldType:gf-review-date "2024-02-19"^^xsd:date ;    # Date
  aqFieldType:gf-approved    "true"^^xsd:boolean ;       # Checkbox
  aqFieldType:gf-case        "https://ardoq.com/"^^xsd:anyURI ;  # Url
  aqFieldType:gf-lifecycle   "Live" .                    # List, so xsd:string
```

Three rules govern how the lexical form is produced.

**A `SelectMultipleList` value is an array, and becomes one triple per option.**

```turtle
aqComponent:app-001
  aqFieldType:gf-data-type "Customer Financial Data" ,
                           "Transaction and Payment Data" .
```

Not one literal holding both. Option labels contain spaces, so a single collapsed
literal could not be split back into the options it came from.

**A `Number` is never written in exponent form.** Values arrive as JSON numbers,
so a cost of 73218541 must be written `"73218541"`, not `"7.3218541e+07"` — the
latter is both a wrong string and an invalid `xsd:decimal`.

**A value that does not fit its field type's datatype is written as a plain
string, not as an invalid typed literal.** `global_field.type` is unconstrained
text and the values are jsonb, so a `Number` field can hold `"n/a"`. GraphLake
rejects a literal whose lexical form does not match its datatype, and a batch of
ops is applied as one update — so emitting one invalid literal would fail the
whole update and stall that store's stream. The fallback is logged with the
schema, entity and field name so the source data can be fixed.

```

Ardoq's frontend collapses the pair into one field of type `DateOnlyRange` or
`DateTimeRange`, and the syncer does the same, so the graph shows the one field a
person sees rather than the two rows the database holds.

**The start row publishes the whole range, under its own IRI.** That identity is
Ardoq's choice, not this repo's: `collapse-date-range-field` gives the collapsed
field the start field's `_id` and `field_view` reports it, so a consumer holding a
range field's id from Ardoq's API matches the IRI here. It also means the field's
model-field links and type constraints need no rewriting.

**The end row publishes nothing at all** — no property, no shape, no model field,
no type constraint. Its dates are inside the start field's interval literal, so a
property of its own would be the same fact under a second predicate.

```turtle
aqFieldType:gf-live-start a aqModel:CustomFieldType, owl:Class, owl:DatatypeProperty ;
  aqModel:id        "gf-live-start" ;   # still the start row's _id
  aqModel:name      "live" ;            # the suffix removed
  aqModel:fieldType "DateOnlyRange" ;   # Ardoq's word for the collapsed field
  rdfs:label        "Live" .

aqShape:ef16e9dc-b8a6-55e7-b25a-8104184f799b a sh:PropertyShape ;
  sh:path aqFieldType:gf-live-start ;
  sh:datatype <http://graphlake.net/types/iso8601-date-interval> .
```

A value is one ISO 8601 interval: two endpoints separated by a slash, both dates
or both dateTimes. **Either side may be empty**, because a range with only a start
is ordinary data — a subscription nobody has cancelled — rather than an incomplete
row:

```turtle
aqComponent:app-001
  aqFieldType:gf-live-start "2024-01-01/2024-12-31"^^glType:iso8601-date-interval .

# 2024-01-01/    still running, no end date
# /2024-12-31    ended, no recorded start
```

Neither half set writes no triple. `"/"` carries no information and GraphLake
rejects it outright, which would fail the whole update it arrived in.

The two endpoints are rendered for the field's own collapsed type rather than for
whatever each value looks like, because GraphLake rejects an interval whose sides
are different kinds. A `DateOnlyRange` holding a value with a time in it therefore
writes two dates, the same truncation an ordinary `Date` field makes.

`gl:intervalStart` and `gl:intervalEnd` read the endpoints back as typed
`xsd:date` / `xsd:dateTime` literals, and an open end comes back unbound:

```sparql
PREFIX gl: <http://graphlake.net/functions/>
SELECT ?c WHERE {
  ?c aqFieldType:gf-live-start ?live .
  FILTER(gl:intervalStart(?live) <= "2024-06-01"^^xsd:date)
  FILTER(!BOUND(gl:intervalEnd(?live)) || gl:intervalEnd(?live) >= "2024-06-01"^^xsd:date)
}
```

**Which rows are endpoints is decided from the one row**, by the type, the name
suffix and the label suffix together — Ardoq's own test
(`date-range-start-field?`). The label matters as much as the name: a customer may
legitimately call a plain `Date` field `contract_end_date`, and only the
`.EndDate` label says the frontend created it as half of a range.

Deciding per row rather than by pairing the two is deliberate. Pairing would mean
holding the sibling's state on all three ingest paths, and on the streaming path
the events arrive one at a time, so a start field seen before its end existed
would publish the uncollapsed form and need retracting later. Two things follow
from the choice:

- An **orphaned end row** — one whose start row is missing, which Ardoq's own
  metamodel refactoring can leave behind — publishes nothing, rather than
  reverting to a plain `Date` field. Its values go with it.
- An **orphaned start row** publishes a range whose values are always open at the
  end.

One narrow gap is left on the streaming path. Renaming an ordinary `Date` field
*into* an endpoint retracts its property, but a model field or type constraint
already pointing at it is only corrected by the next full sync: nothing emits an
event for those rows when the field they name is renamed.

The datatype table above is lossy in one direction. Seven Ardoq types — `Text`,
`TextArea`, `List`, `SelectMultipleList`, `Email`, `User` and `File` — all become
`xsd:string`, so a consumer reading only `sh:datatype` cannot tell a free-text field
from a single-select list from an email address. Advanced search needs that
distinction to choose an editor and a filter for the field.

```turtle

  aqModel:fieldType "List" .           # global_field.type, unaltered
```

Both, not one: `sh:datatype` is what a value must validate against, `aqModel:fieldType`
is what Ardoq calls the field. A field with no type writes no triple.

`global_field.numberFormatOptions` is a jsonb column carried as one string literal.
It holds a format name on most fields and an option object on some, so both shapes
reach the graph:

```turtle
aqFieldType:revenue
  aqModel:fieldType           "Number" ;
  aqModel:numberFormatOptions "currencyUSD" .   # jsonb string "currencyUSD"

aqFieldType:cost
  aqModel:fieldType           "Number" ;
  aqModel:numberFormatOptions "{\"decimals\":2,\"suffix\":\" USD\"}" .
```

One literal rather than a predicate per option. The option set is Ardoq's and this
repo does not own it, so decomposing it would invent vocabulary here and silently
drop whatever Ardoq adds to it next.

**The literal is the column's value, not its JSON serialisation.** A jsonb string is
serialised with its quoting — `"currencyUSD"` — and that quoting is Postgres's
spelling rather than part of the value, so it is not published. Ardoq's own code
writes and reads a format name as a plain string, and a consumer given
`"currencyUSD"` would not recognise it.

**The lexical form is canonicalised, and has to be.** The column reaches the mapper
in two shapes: as text on the snapshot path, which is how pgx renders jsonb, and
decoded on the CDC and history paths. Neither an object nor a scalar agrees across
the two on its own.

- Postgres orders jsonb keys by length then bytes and Go's encoder orders them

  object read from a CDC event would be two different literals.
- A string carries its quoting in the serialised text and none once decoded, so one
  format would reach the graph as `"currencyUSD"` through a full resync and

  organisation at once because it depends on which route last wrote each field.

deliberately the lossy one — plain `json.Unmarshal`, numbers through float64 —

insert the first time any unrelated column changed.

worse than carrying an odd one.

# RDF 1.2 reification and triple terms

GraphLake implements the [RDF 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf12-concepts/#section-triple-terms-reification)
reification model and the corresponding [SPARQL 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/sparql12-query/)
surface syntax.

## Model

- A **triple term** `<<( s p o )>>` denotes a proposition. It may appear **only
  in object position** and is **not asserted** by its presence.
- A triple term is reified by an ordinary, queryable triple
  `reifier rdf:reifies <<( s p o )>>`
  (`rdf:reifies` = `http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#reifies`). The
  subject is the **reifier**; properties about the statement attach to it.
- A reification does **not** entail the triple. Reifying `s p o` does not assert
  `s p o`.
- A triple may have **multiple distinct reifiers** — several independent
  statements/annotations about the same proposition.

Triple identity is content-based: `<<( s p o )>>` is the same term wherever it
appears with the same `s`, `p`, `o`. Internally the components are kept in a
private index so terms can be reconstructed and matched. That index lives in a
graph named `urn:graphlake:quoted`, which is not part of your data: a query that
names no graph does not see it, it is not offered by `GRAPH ?g` or the graph
listing, it is skipped by import and export, and writes to it are refused.

It is hidden rather than sealed. A query that names the graph explicitly reads
it, which is there for inspecting a store when reification misbehaves:

```sparql
SELECT ?s ?p ?o WHERE { GRAPH <urn:graphlake:quoted> { ?s ?p ?o } }
```

Nothing about the index is API. Its contents, and whether it exists at all, may
change; do not build on it.

## SPARQL surface syntax

| Form | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `<<( s p o )>>` | triple term (object position only; not asserted) |
| `<< s p o >>` | reified triple: asserts `s p o`, binds a fresh reifier |
| `<< s p o ~ r >>` | reified triple with explicit reifier `r` |
| `s p o {\| q v \|}` | annotation: asserts `s p o`, attaches `q v` to a fresh reifier |

In a **data** context (`INSERT`/`INSERT DATA`/`CONSTRUCT` templates) a bare
reified triple asserts the inner triple and mints a fresh blank-node reifier per
occurrence. In a **query** pattern the reifier is a non-distinguished variable,
so `<< s p o >>` matches any reifier of that triple, and the inner triple is not
required to be asserted.

### Functions

- `TRIPLE(s, p, o)` — construct a triple term.
- `isTRIPLE(x)` — test whether `x` is a triple term.
- `SUBJECT(t)`, `PREDICATE(t)`, `OBJECT(t)` — extract a triple term's components
  (accepts a triple term or a bound triple-term value).

### Examples

```sparql
# Annotate a statement with provenance.
INSERT DATA {
  << :alice :knows :bob ~ :stmt1 >> :source :crm .
  :stmt1 :recordedAt "2026-01-01"^^xsd:date .
}

# Find who recorded a statement about :alice knowing :bob.
SELECT ?who WHERE {
  ?r rdf:reifies <<( :alice :knows :bob )>> .
  ?r :source ?who .
}

# Bind the embedded components of a reified triple.
SELECT ?s ?p ?o WHERE { ?r rdf:reifies <<( ?s ?p ?o )>> . }

# Delete a reifier and its annotations (the asserted fact is left intact, since
# a reification does not entail the triple). Match the reifier with a variable
# rather than the << >> sugar: in a DELETE the bare << s p o >> would mint a
# fresh blank-node reifier that matches nothing.
DELETE WHERE {
  ?r rdf:reifies <<( :alice :knows :bob )>> .
  ?r ?p ?o .
}
```

All of the above also applies to SPARQL Update: `INSERT`/`INSERT DATA` accept the
full surface syntax (asserting the fact and minting/binding reifiers), and
`DELETE`/`DELETE WHERE` remove reifiers and annotations via the canonical
`rdf:reifies` form.

## Import / export

- **N-Triples**: triple-term objects `<<( s p o )>>` are imported and exported.
  N-Triples has no `~` / `{| |}` sugar (those are Turtle/SPARQL surface syntax),
  so a reified statement is written explicitly as the asserted fact plus a
  `reifier rdf:reifies <<( s p o )>>` triple plus any annotation triples on the
  reifier:

  ```ntriples
  # the asserted fact
  <http://ex/s> <http://ex/p> <http://ex/o> .
  # a reifier of that fact, carrying provenance
  _:r <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#reifies> <<( <http://ex/s> <http://ex/p> <http://ex/o> )>> .
  _:r <http://ex/source> <http://ex/doc1> .
  ```

  Each additional reifier of the same triple is another `rdf:reifies` line —
  that is how parallel statements/annotations are expressed.
- **Turtle export** emits the same N-Triples-compatible triple-term form.
- **Turtle import** of triple-term / `~` / `{| |}` syntax is **not yet
  supported**: the Turtle reader is the third-party `knakk/rdf` parser

  tracked separately.

package core

import (
	"crypto/sha256"
	"encoding/base64"
	"unsafe"
)

const (
	TripleIdPrefix = "urn:x-triple:"
	PrefixLen      = len(TripleIdPrefix)
	HashLen        = 32 // For SHA-256
)

var (
	tripleIDSeparator = []byte("|")
	tripleIDTrue      = []byte("true")
	tripleIDFalse     = []byte("false")
)

// GetTripleId returns a triple's internal identity: the prefix followed by the
// raw SHA-256 digest of its fields. The digest is not encoded, so the result is
// a byte string and NOT valid UTF-8 — it is a map key and a bloom-filter key,
// never a value that reaches a client. Anything stored as RDF data or put on
// the wire must use the text form instead (TripleTermID, GetTransportTripleId).
//
// The raw form is load-bearing: triple-id bloom filters already written into
// .bin.meta files are built over these exact bytes, so re-encoding here would
// make every existing filter miss and silently drop rows from query results.
func GetTripleId(t *Triple) []byte {
	h := sha256.New()
	writeTripleIDString(h, t.Subject)
	writeTripleIDSeparator(h)
	if t.Predicate != nil {
		writeTripleIDString(h, *t.Predicate)
	}
	writeTripleIDSeparator(h)
	writeTripleIDString(h, t.Object)
	writeTripleIDSeparator(h)
	writeTripleIDString(h, t.Datatype)
	writeTripleIDSeparator(h)
	writeTripleIDString(h, t.Lang)
	writeTripleIDSeparator(h)
	if t.IsLiteral {
		_, _ = h.Write(tripleIDTrue)
	} else {
		_, _ = h.Write(tripleIDFalse)
	}
	result := make([]byte, PrefixLen, PrefixLen+HashLen)
	copy(result, TripleIdPrefix)
	return h.Sum(result)
}

func writeTripleIDString(h interface{ Write([]byte) (int, error) }, s string) {
	if s == "" {
		return
	}
	_, _ = h.Write(unsafe.Slice(unsafe.StringData(s), len(s)))
}

// The month is labelled with the date of its latest change rather than with
	// the start of the bucket, so the label says when the state it holds was
	// actually true.
	date := bucketStart.UTC()
	if latest := metricsLatestDate(ordered); !latest.IsZero() {
		date = latest.UTC()
	}
	stats.NewestMonth = date
	// A month that is already there counts as reaching GraphLake: the
	// rows-in-nothing-out contradiction is about a run that wrote nothing
	// anywhere, not about one that had nothing left to write.
	stats.GraphLakeTouched = true
	if snapshotID, alreadyThere := published[snapshotDate(date)]; alreadyThere {

		log.Info().
			Str("schema", schema).
			Str("store", storeID).
			Time("month", date).
			Int64("snapshot_id", snapshotID).
			Msg("history month already on the branch; folded into the state and not published again")
		return stats, nil

## GraphLake SPARQL SELECT returns XML unless Accept names JSON; JWTs expire after 15 minutes

- **Kind:** trap
- **Applies to:** any client of GraphLake `POST /stores/:store/query` / `GET /stores/:store/sparql`
- **Source:** graphlake origin/main web/query.go:41-43 (`acceptsJSONResults`), 860-882 (JSON vs XML fallback); security/manager.go:1262 (15-minute `ExpiresAt`); web/middleware.go:54-66
- **Confidence:** verified
- **Nugget:** Send `Accept: application/sparql-results+json` (or `application/json`); a missing/other Accept yields `application/sparql-results+xml`. Tokens from `POST /admin/authenticate/password` expire after 15 minutes, so long-running clients must re-login (or use `/admin/authenticate/jwt`) on 401. `branch` defaults to `main` when the query param is absent.
- **Comment:** ardoq-api's default branch is `master` (origin/main does not exist there); graphlake and ardoq-docker differ (graphlake uses origin/main, ardoq-docker origin/master).

---
name: save-nugget
version: 1.0.0
description: Record a durable, cross-cutting finding about a repo — an unusual convention, a documented "do X this way" rule, a structural principle, a test/build peculiarity, a known exception — into the agent workspace's nuggets/ directory so any later agent can find it. Trigger when you (or an agent you are running as) hit a piece of information that is not specific to the current task but that other agents would want to know before writing or reviewing code in this repo. Always checks the existing nuggets of other agents for the same fact before writing, so nuggets are not duplicated. Not for task findings, not for obvious practices, and never a place to record conclusions about the work in progress.
argument-hint: [optional: the nugget in a sentence]
allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash
---

# Save nugget

Capture one durable fact about the codebase into the shared workspace nuggets, with its source, so the next agent does not have to rediscover it.

A **nugget** is information that is *about the repo*, not about your task: a convention, a rule, a structural principle, a peculiarity, an explicit instruction found in documentation. It outlives the task that surfaced it and is useful to **any** agent — an augmentor about to write code, an enforcer judging conventions, an investigator orienting itself.

## What qualifies

Save it if another agent, arriving cold, would write worse code or waste effort without knowing it:

- **Unusual or repo-specific conventions** — a naming, layering, module or error-handling pattern that is consistent here but not standard practice generally.
- **Explicit documented instructions** — a README/CONTRIBUTING/CLAUDE.md/ADR/wiki page that states "do X this way" or "never do Y". Note where it says so.
- **Structural principles** — what lives in which layer or package and why; what the boundary rules are; where a given kind of code is registered.
- **Test, build and tooling peculiarities** — how tests must be run here, a fixture/harness requirement, a lint rule that bites, a generated artifact that must be regenerated rather than edited.
- **Exceptions and traps** — a place that deliberately violates the general rule, a deprecated path that still looks current, a helper that must be used instead of the obvious inline approach, an abstraction that is load-bearing in a non-obvious way.

## What does NOT qualify

- **Anything specific to the task at hand.** Findings that answer your current question belong in your report to your parent, not here. This is the most common misuse.
- Conclusions, plans, progress, or status of work in flight.
- General software practice that is not specific to this codebase.
- Anything already stated in a `CLAUDE.md`, or plainly visible from a file's name or location.
- A restatement of what some code does. A nugget is a rule or a principle, not a description of one function.
- Speculation. If you have not verified it, do not save it. "Two files do this" is a pattern worth one careful look, not yet a convention.

## Workflow

### 1. Locate the workspace

The agent workspace is the directory that sits alongside the repo roots and holds the `specs/` folder — in the Ardoq checkout that is `.aispace/`, but the name varies, so detect it rather than assuming:

```bash
# walk up from the working directory looking for the workspace
d=$PWD; while [ "$d" != "/" ]; do
  for c in "$d"/.aispace; do [ -d "$c" ] && echo "$c"; done
  d=$(dirname "$d"); done
```

Prefer a candidate that contains `specs/`. If several exist, pick the one nearest the repos you are working in. If none exists, do not invent a location elsewhere — create `nuggets/` inside the workspace the parent named, or ask.

Nugget files live in `<workspace>/nuggets/`. Create the directory if it is missing.

### 2. Check for duplication — before writing anything

Read what is already recorded. This is mandatory: the nugget files are shared, and a second copy of a known fact makes the whole set less trustworthy.

```bash
ls <workspace>/nuggets/
grep -ril "<distinctive keyword from your nugget>" <workspace>/nuggets/
```

Search on the distinctive terms of the fact itself — the namespace, helper, flag, file or rule name — not on your phrasing of it. Then read the files that hit. Outcomes:

- **Already recorded, same fact** → do not save. Say so in your report and move on.
- **Recorded but you have verified it more precisely, or found the authoritative source it lacked** → add the refinement to **your own** file, with a one-line cross-reference to the existing note (`See also: nuggets/<file>.md — "<nugget title>"`).
- **Recorded and now wrong or outdated** → record the correction in **your own** file, cite your evidence, and cross-reference the stale note. State plainly that it contradicts the earlier one.
- **Not recorded** → save it.

**Never edit or delete another agent's nugget file.** You only ever append to your own. Reconciling and reorganising the collected nuggets is a separate job.

### 3. Write it

One file per agent. Name it `<agent-type>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>.md`, timestamped at the agent's first nugget, e.g. `nuggets/investigator-20260916-143210.md`. If you save several nuggets during one run, **append** to that same file rather than creating more.

File header, written once:

```markdown
# Nuggets — <agent-type>, <YYYY-MM-DD>

Context: <one clause naming what this agent was doing when it found these — enough to judge the finding's provenance, no more.>
```

SKILL.md
---
name: save-nugget
version: 1.0.0
description: Record a durable, cross-cutting finding about a repo — an unusual convention, a documented "do X this way" rule, a structural principle, a test/build peculiarity, a known exception — into the agent workspace's nuggets/ directory so any later agent can find it. Trigger when you (or an agent you are running as) hit a piece of information that is not specific to the current task but that other agents would want to know before writing or reviewing code in this repo. Always checks the existing nuggets of other agents for the same fact before writing, so nuggets are not duplicated. Not for task findings, not for obvious practices, and never a place to record conclusions about the work in progress.
argument-hint: [optional: the nugget in a sentence]
allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash
---

# Save nugget

Capture one durable fact about the codebase into the shared workspace nuggets, with its source, so the next agent does not have to rediscover it.

A **nugget** is information that is *about the repo*, not about your task: a convention, a rule, a structural principle, a peculiarity, an explicit instruction found in documentation. It outlives the task that surfaced it and is useful to **any** agent — an augmentor about to write code, an enforcer judging conventions, an investigator orienting itself.

## What qualifies

Save it if another agent, arriving cold, would write worse code or waste effort without knowing it:

- **Unusual or repo-specific conventions** — a naming, layering, module or error-handling pattern that is consistent here but not standard practice generally.
- **Explicit documented instructions** — a README/CONTRIBUTING/CLAUDE.md/ADR/wiki page that states "do X this way" or "never do Y". Note where it says so.
- **Structural principles** — what lives in which layer or package and why; what the boundary rules are; where a given kind of code is registered.
- **Test, build and tooling peculiarities** — how tests must be run here, a fixture/harness requirement, a lint rule that bites, a generated artifact that must be regenerated rather than edited.
- **Exceptions and traps** — a place that deliberately violates the general rule, a deprecated path that still looks current, a helper that must be used instead of the obvious inline approach, an abstraction that is load-bearing in a non-obvious way.

## What does NOT qualify

- **Anything specific to the task at hand.** Findings that answer your current question belong in your report to your parent, not here. This is the most common misuse.
- Conclusions, plans, progress, or status of work in flight.
- General software practice that is not specific to this codebase.
- Anything already stated in a `CLAUDE.md`, or plainly visible from a file's name or location.
- A restatement of what some code does. A nugget is a rule or a principle, not a description of one function.
- Speculation. If you have not verified it, do not save it. "Two files do this" is a pattern worth one careful look, not yet a convention.

## Workflow

### 1. Locate the workspace

The agent workspace is the directory that sits alongside the repo roots and holds the `specs/` folder — in the Ardoq checkout that is `.aispace/`, but the name varies, so detect it rather than assuming:

```bash
# walk up from the working directory looking for the workspace
d=$PWD; while [ "$d" != "/" ]; do
  for c in "$d"/.aispace; do [ -d "$c" ] && echo "$c"; done
  d=$(dirname "$d"); done
```

Prefer a candidate that contains `specs/`. If several exist, pick the one nearest the repos you are working in. If none exists, do not invent a location elsewhere — create `nuggets/` inside the workspace the parent named, or ask.

Nugget files live in `<workspace>/nuggets/`. Create the directory if it is missing.

### 2. Check for duplication — before writing anything

Read what is already recorded. This is mandatory: the nugget files are shared, and a second copy of a known fact makes the whole set less trustworthy.

```bash
ls <workspace>/nuggets/
grep -ril "<distinctive keyword from your nugget>" <workspace>/nuggets/
```

Search on the distinctive terms of the fact itself — the namespace, helper, flag, file or rule name — not on your phrasing of it. Then read the files that hit. Outcomes:

- **Already recorded, same fact** → do not save. Say so in your report and move on.
- **Recorded but you have verified it more precisely, or found the authoritative source it lacked** → add the refinement to **your own** file, with a one-line cross-reference to the existing note (`See also: nuggets/<file>.md — "<nugget title>"`).
- **Recorded and now wrong or outdated** → record the correction in **your own** file, cite your evidence, and cross-reference the stale note. State plainly that it contradicts the earlier one.
- **Not recorded** → save it.

**Never edit or delete another agent's nugget file.** You only ever append to your own. Reconciling and reorganising the collected nuggets is a separate job.

### 3. Write it

One file per agent. Name it `<agent-type>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>.md`, timestamped at the agent's first nugget, e.g. `nuggets/investigator-20260916-143210.md`. If you save several nuggets during one run, **append** to that same file rather than creating more.

File header, written once:

```markdown
# Nuggets — <agent-type>, <YYYY-MM-DD>

Context: <one clause naming what this agent was doing when it found these — enough to judge the finding's provenance, no more.>
```

Then one block per nugget:

```markdown
## <short, declarative title stating the rule>

- **Kind:** convention | structure | documented-rule | test | build | exception | trap
- **Applies to:** <repo, package or path scope this holds within>
- **Source:** <path/to/file.clj:120> · <doc path or URL> · <command whose output shows it>
- **Confidence:** verified in N places | stated in documentation | single instance, unconfirmed
- **Nugget:** <the rule, stated as a rule in one or two sentences>
- **Comment:** <optional: why it matters, when it does not apply, what breaks if ignored>
```

Rules for the content:

- **State it as a rule**, in the imperative or as a general fact — not as a story about how you found it.
- **Always cite a source** a later agent can open: `file:line`, a doc path, a URL, or the exact command. A nugget without a source is not usable.
- **Be honest about confidence.** Mark a single unconfirmed instance as such rather than promoting it to a convention.
- **Scope it.** A rule that holds only in one package must say so; an over-broad nugget is worse than none.
- **Keep it short.** A few lines. No background, no narrative, no code blocks unless the exact text *is* the rule.

### 4. Report it in one line

Tell your parent, briefly: what you saved and where (`saved nugget "<title>" → nuggets/<file>.md`), or that the fact was already recorded. Never let the nugget displace or pad the answer your parent actually asked for.
